analysis.one_liner: Taxes 95% of large corporations' profits above their pre-pandemic levels through 2026.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, amendment, or vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a 95% tax on the "excess profits" of corporations with at least $500 million in average annual gross receipts — meaning profits above what the company earned, adjusted for inflation, in 2015 through 2019. It would apply to tax years beginning after 2023 and expire after 2026. It also closes a few tax techniques large companies use, such as a deduction for offshore intangible income and a depreciation method that delays taxes, and it limits how much executive pay any company can deduct. The revenue would go to the Treasury; the bill does not dedicate it to any specific program.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in the general sense that revenue raised from large corporations flows to the Treasury, where it could reduce deficits or offset other taxes. The bill does not earmark the money for any program. The Framers' stated aim was to recapture profits companies earned by raising prices during and after the pandemic, so consumers who paid those higher prices would benefit if the tax deterred such pricing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General taxpayers via new federal revenue

how_it_helps.text: It taxes 95% of a large corporation's profits above its inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average, in addition to normal income tax, through 2026.
It applies only to corporations averaging at least $500 million in annual gross receipts, measured with related companies treated as one, so mid-sized and small businesses are untouched.

It broadens the tax base for covered companies by disallowing certain deductions (including for offshore intangible income and accelerated depreciation) and by limiting the tax deduction for pay to a wider set of highly paid executives, not just top officers.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and, through them, their shareholders. A company that earned far more in 2024-2026 than in its 2015-2019 baseline would pay up to 95% of that excess, capped at 75% of its modified taxable income for the year. Some of the cost could be passed to consumers through prices or absorbed in lower investment and returns.

drawbacks.text: A 95% rate on profits above the baseline is close to confiscatory and could discourage companies from expanding output or investing in the United States during the covered years, since extra profit would be almost entirely taxed away.

The baseline (inflation-adjusted average of 2015-2019 profits) may not reflect a company's current legitimate costs or market conditions, so some of what counts as 'excess' profit could be ordinary earnings today.
The bill applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2023, even though it was introduced in July 2024, meaning it would change tax liability retroactively for a year already underway.

It exempts regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and S corporations, which creates gaps where differently structured firms earning the same money would pay nothing under the new tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — taxing windfall profits above a pre-pandemic baseline — is a real policy used in other countries and wartime America, and it targets the companies that posted record profits while prices rose. But this version is aggressive: a 95% rate over a 2015-2019 baseline is far steeper than comparable windfall taxes, the retroactive start date raises fairness concerns, and the carve-outs for REITs and S corporations invite reorganization to escape the tax. The bill also never says what the money is for. As drafted, the design weaknesses are significant even for a supporter of the concept.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on July 9, 2024, with Senator Ed Markey as its sole cosponsor.
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills that receive no further action die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with over $500 million in annual receipts and their shareholders are better off, because they will pay no excess-profits tax; the relatively small number of members who backed the bill gained attention but no policy change.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it as its sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Republican caucus
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill or moved it forward.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split was recorded; the only support on paper came from an Independent sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Large corporations (over $500M average annual gross receipts)
industries.note: These companies would pay up to 95% of profits above their inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average, on top of regular income tax, through 2026. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against taxpayers who would otherwise receive the revenue.

industries.industry: REITs, regulated investment companies, and S corporations
industries.note: The bill exempts these structures entirely, so identical profits earned through them would escape the excess-profits tax paid by conventional corporations — an advantage for their investors that comes at the revenue's expense.
A new 95% excess-profits tax with a five-year baseline would generate heavy demand for tax planning and structuring work. This effect was mooted because the bill never advanced.
